extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and creators working in genre fiction across novels, comics, film, TV, animation, and picture books
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for how genre and narrative medium create expectations (promises) for readers/viewers and how writers should use those promises to shape satisfying stories. Covers specific genre beats (romance, cozy mystery, superhero) and medium-specific storytelling tools (novel POV, animation visuals, film editing/camera/sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre as a promise
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre of your story is making promises to the reader, and the medium upon which your story is told makes promises too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genres (both bookshelf genres and elemental genres) set expectations right from the outset; writers should recognize and leverage those promises to ensure they deliver a satisfying story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance: happily ever after / happy-for-now
rubrics_metrics.description: “If your romance novel doesn’t have happily ever after or a happy at least for now, it’s not a romance novel.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romance readers expect a HEA or at minimum a happy-at-the-end (happy-for-now). Failing to provide that core promise means you are not meeting the genre's fundamental contract with the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cozy mystery: murder, contained world, and safe resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Cozy mystery has very strict beats: there is going to be a murder; the world is contained and safe; the story solves the puzzle and at the end "it’s all okay again."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences expect puzzles they can solve, familiar setting/characters, and the assurance that favorite characters (and pets) remain safe; violating these expectations (e.g., killing a beloved main character instead of retiring them) can deeply upset the audience (example: Death in Paradise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superhero genre: epic fights and satisfying matchups
rubrics_metrics.description: Superhero stories promise epic fights that feel weighted and show interesting matchups (bracketing who fights whom); audiences want to see how different powers and characters interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasoned, varied, and visually/structurally interesting confrontations; avoid lazy mirrored-power stand-ins that make fights feel boring (e.g., villain as a chunkier version of the hero). Use fight sequencing to satisfy audience curiosity about matchups (Civil War, Avengers examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hit the genre beats audiences expect
rubrics_metrics.description: Many genres (cozy mystery, romance, police procedural, etc.) have specific beats and moments that readers expect to be delivered where they expect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the beats of the genre you’re writing; missing those beats will make audiences anxious or upset. Use those beats deliberately to satisfy genre promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium promise — novels: internal POV and narrative access
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels (especially third-person limited) can give direct internal access to a character's thoughts and inner life in ways other media struggle to replicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the novel form to show internal states and thought processes; recognize that film/TV must rely on other tools (voiceover, acting, visual shorthand) to approach the same effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium promise — animation: visual design and audience signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Animation carries promises about how it will tell story visually and often signals intended audience via design cues (e.g., bigger heads/bigger eyes for kids; smaller heads/smaller eyes for adult-targeted work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animation can change character design over time to show arc (Centaurworld example). Visual design often communicates part of the story; use design intentionally to set expectations and deliver story beats visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture books: words and art create a third thing
rubrics_metrics.description: In picture books the art and the words will interact to create a third thing which is the story; writers should avoid over-describing and trust illustrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let illustrations carry narrative information rather than repeating everything in text; coordinate text and art to combine into a single storytelling experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lore mining: reward background visuals and hidden detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual media (animation, TV, comics) can include background visuals, Easter eggs, and clues that reward viewers who 'lore mine' and add depth to the world (Gravity Falls example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide meaningful background details that enrich the story for engaged viewers; these elements can create long-term audience engagement and discovery beyond the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kuleshov effect: sequencing informs emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kuleshov effect: even a neutral face can be read differently depending on the shot that follows it; sequencing of images informs the audience how to interpret emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editing and shot sequence deliberately to shape audience perception of characters' feelings and intentions rather than relying on a single face or image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all the tools of the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media have different toolsets (actor performance, camera placement, cutting pace, background sound, scoring, lighting, animation design); successful storytelling uses all relevant tools together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on a single element (e.g., actor face or a visual homage) to reproduce the full effect of another medium; when adapting or working within a medium, apply its full palette (camera, acting, editing, sound, music, lighting, visual design) to deliver the promised experience (Cowboy Bebop discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't betray fundamental audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience expectations formed by genre and medium create a contract; breaking central promises (such as character safety in a cozy or HEA in romance) feels like a betrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend to subvert expectations, do so with awareness and craft; otherwise, meet the core promises or change the genre/medium so the promise aligns with your story's deliverables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and align your deliverable with genre/medium (homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: What do you plan to have your work-in-progress deliver? Does the genre or medium you’re working in support the promise of that deliverable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not, write a one-page outline changing the genre or medium to support the promise you’re making. This is practical advice to ensure alignment between intended story deliverables and the expectations of the chosen genre/medium.
